body_markdown:
Whether by participating or spectating, there’s no doubt that our readers love motorsports. The stories collected after our[initial question](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/whats-your-favorite-race-track-experience/#comments) were wonderful, as they were a great mix of personal recollections and experiences with famous folks from across the automotive hobby.


So without any further ado, let’s see what everyone said about their favorite moments on a racetrack!


**buster51:** I don’t remember what year exactly, but around 1970-72 I was standing along the rail at the top end at Lebanon Valley, NY drag strip. Don Garlits blew by me. I could feel the pounding in my chest, and the soda foamed out of the can.


**MACE:** My future wife and I went to Ascot for the non-winged sprint car show to celebrate my birthday. When we sat down in our usual section, she produced a birthday cake, placed and lit candles. She started singing “Happy Birthday,” and all the TURN ONE CROWD JOINED IN singing. We handed out cake to as many of “our people” as we could!


**Mike L:** We used to go watch dirt track racing at Tri City Speedway in Granite City, IL. Probably the most memorable thing was during an A Main for the World of Outlaws. A rookie driver was leading, but then the King of the Dirt, Steve Kinser, took the kid to school with a pass in turn one that few other drivers could pull off, and (of course) went on to win the feature.


Something that always impressed me about Kinser was, no matter how late the races ended, and no matter how far he had to go to race the next night, he ALWAYS stayed until the last autograph was signed, especially for the kids.


**[Paul Stenquist:](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/paul-stenquist/)** More than half a century ago, when I was mechanic and engine builder for the QuVoe Charger funny car and owner/driver Ed O’Brien, we beat the NHRA world champ Shirl Greer in the first round of an eight-car show at the Hollywood, Florida, drag strip—6.68, 225 mph to Greer’s 6.69 at a similar speed. It was the biggest thrill of my life thus far, but I’m hoping to top it one of these days.


Bettmann Archive/Getty Images


**Mike H:** 1980, USGP at Watkins Glen. I saw a tall blond guy in a Toyota jacket in the pits before the start of qualifying. I told Dan Gurney that I had never asked for an autograph before, but I wanted his. We chatted, then we walked together down the line of F1 cars waiting to qualify.


He told me what was unique about each of the cars. When we got to the Alfas, which were lined up first and second for quali, he said, “I don’t know how they can use so many exotic metals and make them so heavy.” Sad for me to hear, since I’m an Alfa guy, but Giacomelli went out and put the Alfa on the pole. Nearly as great an experience was seeing Gurney win at Spa on my first wedding anniversary in 1967.


**studenorton:** About any Midwest track, just as the lights come on for the A Main, the sprinters bunch up by 3s or 4s for a salute lap. Most of their colors didn’t exist in nature, or before Technicolor. It is the most vivid sight in all of sport.


Cameron Neveu


**LD:** My favourite moment was at the demolition derby where my BIL would bring his car to the field in a 40-yard bin, fire it up inside the bin, and then swing open the doors and drive it out. The amused patrons would see an AMC Hornet or Gremlin with the number “1/2” on the side. His logic was that he could manoeuvre better in the smaller vehicle, and he always made the top 3.


**buster51:** 1976-78 F1 at Watkins Glen, NY, standing in the rain along the longest straight and being able to hear the Ferraris scream by and brake for the corner. In those days, the mechanics worked all night. You could walk through an aisle in the center of the garage and watch and talk to them, and they’d hand out souvenirs. I still have a pair of Lotus brake pads on my dresser. They’re probably the size of a business card.


**Bill G:** There are a lot of favorite track time memories for me, starting with seeing and hearing the new 962s at Road Atlanta and my first HDPE at Roebling. But the best times were talking to Hurley Haywood at Roebling at a vintage race, and most of all getting to have a beer with Paul Newman after a Walter Mitty Challenge race at Road Atlanta. Two incredibly great men!


**Rocco417:** A friend of mine had a son that was doing graphic art for Chrysler at the time and working for some of the top fuel dragster guys, he got use inside the “ropes” and watched them tear down a nitromethane “hemi” and fire it back up. We were all on liquid courage at the time, so we thought nothing of it when all the crew put on gas masks to fire that baby back up. We of course had no masks, but we didn’t care.


This 1970 Ford Mustang Boss 302 embodied the classic Trans Am look.


[Nathan Petroelje](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nathan-petroelje/)


**Tuffy67:** My son and I were fortunate enough to spend the entire Monterey Historic weekend at Laguna Seca with Parnelli Jones the first time he raced his 1970 Championship Trans Am Mustang in an historic race. My good friend owned the car, and we had total access to the Historic group, including long chats with drivers Sam Posey, George Folmer, Sir Sterling Moss, as well as Vic Edelbrock and a chat with Jay Leno.


All of them were wonderful gentlemen, friendly and accommodating. The stories and good-natured jabbing at each other after all the years of competing against and with each other were mind-blowing. My son has often said it was the greatest weekend of his life, and I’m inclined to agree.


**Cozy:** Several years ago I served on the board of a company that helped sponsor a Dreyer and Reinbold car in the Indy 500. One of the perks was being able to mingle with the folks on the starting grid until the very “last minute.” My favorite memory is having my picture taken with “The King,” Richard Petty.


**Gary B:** Hmm, passing a Corvette C6 with a manual transmission in the Supra at Autobahn CC that was clearly on the edge of its stock Goodyear’s traction in the turns and never seeing that car again after a while. Another one was doing a Lexus event at MSR for the dealers and grabbing the lead car and sticking to the rear end of the pro driver leading the event and doing my best to mirror his every move in our V-8-powered performance Lexus cars. We were going fairly spirited, and 4/5ths of the way in, the pro driver realized there was no one behind me and asked if it is ok to slow down for the rest so they could catch up.


I am under no illusion that the pro driver was going 10/10ths or that I am as good as him at that effort, but I was good enough for whatever his effort was for us to lose everyone else. Then again, they were salespeople so maybe that isn’t as impressive a thing to have done but I don’t care as it felt really good.


Eddy Eckart


**Mike M:** My favorite moment was my first win in a SCCA road race. It occurred in my second year of racing. I wouldn’t have been possible without the help of my crew chief, Jeff K.


**Bill D:** Showing up late for a Crazy Eddie night of thrills drag race event at Raceway Park in Englishtown, NJ. A friend and I were in the parking lot behind the grandstand. Just as we got to the far end of the stands, two jet cars took off and blasted down the track. The sight and sound of two ground-based jet cars passing into view I can still remember to this day.


**Richard B:** This may sound mundane, BUT as a long-time corner worker and sometimes driver, the best part of a race day is arriving at the track EARLY in the morning, looking over the paddock and ENJOYING a good cup of coffee in those last peaceful moments before the first engine starts. It’s the anticipation of what unknown things the day is about to deliver


**[Kyle Smith:](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)** Sunrise paddock walks with hot coffee truly are the best.


Mike Powell/Getty Images


**RobH:** I’ve been very fortunate in my life, and I will share a few stories. My wife and I, along with our best friends, were enjoying our 30th wedding anniversary in the South of France, and we took the bus to see the changing of the guard at the palace in Monaco. From up on the hill, we could see the streets of Monte Carlo closed, and we walked down to learn the Historics were going to race the next day (the week preceding the F1), and the streets were closed, and pits were lined with all the F1 cars from years gone by—amazing! Then we walked the closed track, looked at all the boats docked in the harbor, many of them team boats, and then got together at home the next weekend to watch the race and marvel that we had just been there!


From a driving standpoint, I was fortunate that whilst working for a major tire manufacturer that supplied sticky tires to race schools, we hosted customers for two-day events. Getting instruction from expert racers, then carrying out lead-follow laps, with the pro going faster and faster (like Gary above), allowing you to keep up if you could, then realizing you were catching up to your guests and slowing down so as not to lap them… awesome stuff! Sessions always ended with ride-alongs with the pros—you really understand why race car drivers are in such great shape and how the car takes so much abuse going over chicanes, etc.


I have had an amazing life!


**Frank B:** I’ve attended and participated in a great many motorsports events in my 73 years. The one that stands out was my dad taking me to the Wednesday night drag races (bracket races) in 1967 in Wichita, Kansas. I was 14 years old and had my driver’s permit. He convinced the officials to let me race if he rode along, as the driver’s permit stipulated. I got to make a dozen or more passes in his 1957 Dodge Coronet 2-door with a 325 4-bbl and a 3 on the tree. Heady times for a 14-year-old!
